blocks.title: Page 7
blocks.content:
Background 
There were an estimated 10.6 million people who newly developed tuberculosis (TB) in 2022 and of 
the 7.5 million reported cases, 83% involved the lungs (WHO Global Tuberculosis Report 2023). In 
2022, there were about 410,000 new cases of rifampicin-resistant or multidrug resistant TB.  Several 
rapid molecular tests are recommended by the WHO as the initial diagnostic test for TB, some of which 
can detect drug resistance simultaneously (WHO 2022). These tests can be used at the lower levels of 
the health care system. 
 
WHO groups individual tests with similar characteristics a

summary.text: Gives background for the LC-aNAAT review, citing 2022 global estimates of TB incidence and rifampicin-resistant TB and WHO's recommendation of rapid molecular tests as initial diagnostics. It explains WHO's grouping of tests into classes and the clinical importance of detecting rifampicin and isoniazid resistance.

blocks.title: Page 8
blocks.content:
Index tests  
The individual LC-aNAATs are: 
● GeneXpert MTB/RIF Ultra;  
● Truenat (Truenat MTB Plus and Truenat MTB‐RIF Dx);  
● STANDARD M10, SD Biosensor;  
● IRON-qPCR, BIONEER 
For ease of reference, we will refer to GeneXpert MTB/RIF Ultra as Xpert Ultra and the two Truenat 
assays as Truenat except where necessary to refer to a specific assay. 
Xpert Ultra, Cepheid, USA 
Xpert Ultra is a NAAT that functions as an automated closed system that performs real-time 
polymerase chain reaction (PCR). Xpert Ultra can be used for diagnosing TB and RR-TB. Xpert Ultra can 
be performed by operato

summary.text: Lists the index tests in the LC-aNAAT class and describes the Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra and Truenat assays, including how they detect TB, report semi-quantitative results and target the rpoB gene for rifampicin resistance.

blocks.title: Page 9
blocks.content:
The STANDARD M10 is an in vitro molecular diagnostics system that automatically extracts and 
amplifies nucleic acids (DNA, RNA) from the collected samples, and analyses the data from 
amplification in real-time, by combining the processes of isothermal amplification and real-time PCR 
in a single platform using all-in-one cartridge systems. There are two variations currently available for 
TB detection: STANDARD™ M10 MTB/NTM and STANDARD™ M10 MDR-TB. These assays are intended 
for use with the STANDARD M10 system and provide qualitative results within 80 minutes from human 
sputum or sputum s

blocks.title: Page 11
blocks.content:
Culture (microbiological reference standard) 
Culture is considered the best reference standard for TB using either automated liquid culture or solid 
culture methods. Since both culture methods are used interchangeably in clinical practice (Moreira 
2015), a positive result either alone or in combination was accepted as a diagnosis of TB while all 
negative cultures indicated no TB. 
Composite reference standard (CRS) 
We defined CRS as a positive culture or a clinical decision to initiate treatment for PTB (i.e., clinically 
diagnosed PTB). The CRS may be based on the results of microbiologi

summary.text: Defines the culture and composite reference standards, then describes data extraction, quality assessment with QUADAS-2 and planned meta-analyses of sensitivity and specificity by subgroup such as smear and HIV status.

blocks.title: Page 14
blocks.content:
Search Results: Truenat 
We identified 1175 research articles for screening from searches of electronic sources. After removing 
duplicate studies (n=524), we screened the titles and abstracts of 651 unique articles and excluded 
617. We identified four reports through citation searching and WHO call for data. We performed full-
text screening of 38 articles and included five reports of which four contributed to the meta-analysis 
of Truenat MTB Plus and two included for the meta-analysis of rifampicin resistance (Figure 2).

From 37 database records (3 duplicates removed), 34 were screened, 32 excluded and 2 reports assessed for eligibility; both were excluded (an ongoing trial and a conference abstract/case-control study). No studies were included.

blocks.title: Page 15
blocks.content:
Search Results: STANDARD M10 and other index tests 
We screened 34 titles and abstracts and excluded 32. We assessed the full texts of two articles and 
found none eligible for this review (Figure 3).

Characteristics of included studies 
There were 36 included studies: 31 that only evaluated Xpert Ultra (including one study based on two 
reports—Nicol 2018 and Zar 2019—and two studies extracted from a single report—Mishra 2020a & 
2020b), three studies that only evaluated Truenat MTB Plus (Gomathi 2020, Jose 2024, Nga

summary.text: Reports that no eligible studies were found for STANDARD M10 or other new LC-aNAATs and summarizes the 36 included studies, mostly of Xpert Ultra, with eleven assessing rifampicin resistance detection.

blocks.title: Page 16
blocks.content:
Respiratory specimen types 
Most included studies used sputum for their evaluation of LC-aNAATs. Three studies exclusively 
evaluated Xpert Ultra testing of BAL samples (Chien 2020, Park 2019, Zhang 2021) while one study 
included BAL in addition to sputum samples (Sava 2023).  One study (Penn-Nicholson 2021) pooled 
multiple sputum specimens per participant in the reference laboratory and used unpooled sputum in 
the peripheral labs. Sabi 2018 used the best result from multiple specimens (1 to 4) per participant. Li 
2023 used three sputum samples per person and examined each sample microscop

summary.text: Describes the respiratory specimen types used in the included studies, mainly sputum, with some using bronchoalveolar lavage or pooled samples.

blocks.title: Page 29
blocks.content:
The sensitivities in the 10 studies (2127 participants) were between 0% and 96% and the specificities 
were between 96% and 100% (Figure 8). The summary sensitivity (95% CI) was 69.9% (52.7 to 82.9) and 
the summary specificity was 98.8% (96.2 to 99.7).  
 
For a population of 1000 adults and adolescents where 100 have pulmonary tuberculosis on a composite 
reference standard, 80 would be LC-aNAAT-positive and 10 (13%) would not have tuberculosis (false-
positives); 920 would be LC-aNAAT-negative and 30 (3%) would have tuberculosis (false-negatives).

Tuberculosis is one of the top 10 causes of death and a leading cause from a single infectious agent,

during that year, an estimated 10.6 million people developed tuberculosis disease, including around

Globally, extrapulmonary tuberculosis accounted for 20% of the 7.4 million cases of 
tuberculosis notified in 2022, ranging from 8% in the WHO Western Pacific Region to 24% in 
the Eastern Mediterranean Region (WHO Global Tuberculosis Report 2023). In 2022, there 
were about 520,000 new cases of rifampicin-resistant tuberculosis; of these cases, 78% had 
multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (WHO Global Tuberculosis Report 2023). Xpert Ultra and 
Truenat assays are WHO-recommended rapid tests that simultaneously detect tuberculosis and 
rifampicin resistance in people with signs and sym

summary.text: Gives background on extrapulmonary TB, which made up a fifth of notified TB cases in 2022, and on rifampicin-resistant TB. It describes Xpert Ultra's improved detection limit compared with Xpert MTB/RIF and its new trace result category.

of clinical symptoms and history of prior tuberculosis. No rifampicin resistance results are 
available (indeterminate) for people with trace results. As with Xpert MTB/RIF, Xpert Ultra 
detects both live and dead bacteria.

capreomycin), prothionamide and ethionamide. It uses IRON qPCR, which is a single 
instrument for extraction and amplification and detection. Two modules are available per

Discussion 
The sensitivity and specificity of LC-aNAATs for detection of extrapulmonary tuberculosis 
varied with site of disease and specimen type. Based on a microbiological reference standard, 
sensitivity was lowest for detection of peritoneal tuberculosis using peritoneal fluid with a 
summary sensitivity (95% CI) of 50.0% (20.0 to 80.0) and summary specificity (95% CI) of 
98.4% (89.3 to 99.8). Conversely, sensitivity was highest for detection of lymph node 
tuberculosis using lymph node tissue with a summary sensitivity (95% CI) of 96.3% (89.1 to 
98.8) and summary specificity (95% CI)

summary.text: The discussion notes that accuracy varied by disease site and specimen, with sensitivity lowest for peritoneal fluid and highest for lymph node tissue against a microbiological reference. It calls for studies of other LC-aNAATs and notes high-certainty evidence of very high accuracy for rifampicin resistance.

blocks.title: Page 164
blocks.content:
Executive Summary 
 
Background 
WHO recommends Rapid nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs) as the initial diagnostic test 
for tuberculosis (TB), some of which can detect drug resistance simultaneously. They have 
higher diagnostic accuracy than smear microscopy and have fast turnaround times that may 
lead to a positive impact on patient outcomes. 
 
Objective 
To assess the impact of low complexity (LC) and moderate complexity (MC) NAATs compared 
to smear microscopy or culture on patient outcomes in people investigated for TB. 
 
Methods 
We searched several electronic databases from in

summary.text: The executive summary explains that WHO recommends rapid NAATs as initial TB tests and that the review assessed their impact on patient outcomes compared with smear microscopy or culture. It reports trial results on time to diagnosis and treatment, with moderate certainty.

blocks.title: Page 165
blocks.content:
Conclusions 
The use of Xpert Ultra may decrease the time to TB diagnosis and improve the time to TB 
treatment initiation. However, we found that compared to smear microscopy or culture, 
there is limited evidence with moderate certainty of evidence to confidently conclude 
that Xpert Ultra has an impact on patient-important outcomes.

summary.text: Concludes that Xpert Ultra may shorten time to diagnosis and treatment but that evidence of its effect on patient-important outcomes is limited.

blocks.title: Page 166
blocks.content:
Background 
Description of the condition 
TB is one of the leading causes of death worldwide and affects all ages (1). TB is caused by 
Mycobacterium tuberculosis (M. tuberculosis) bacteria. TB primarily affects the respiratory 
system causing pulmonary TB (PTB) but can also affect other organ systems in the form of 
extrapulmonary TB (EPTB). While TB is preventable and largely curable, an estimated 10.6 
million people fell ill with TB worldwide in 2022 and around 1.3 million people died of TB (2, 
3). 
 
Pulmonary TB 
PTB is the most prevalent form of TB. Loss of appetite, weight loss, letha

summary.text: Gives background on TB, noting 10.6 million cases and about 1.3 million deaths in 2022, and describes pulmonary and extrapulmonary forms. It introduces drug-resistant TB as a major global health security threat.

blocks.title: Page 167
blocks.content:
and testing for drug resistance using rapid molecular tests, culture methods or sequencing 
technologies. Resistance to rifampicin—the most effective first-line drug—is of greatest 
concern. Resistance to rifampicin and isoniazid is defined as multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB).  
 
Both MDR-TB and rifampicin-resistant TB (RR-TB) require treatment with second-line drugs 
(3). WHO uses five categories to classify cases of DR-TB: isoniazid-resistant TB, RR-TB, MDR-
TB, extensively drug-resistant TB (XDR-TB) and pre-XDR-TB. 
The definitions for DR-TB have been revised in response to advances in TB t

that functions as an automated closed system that performs real-time polymerase chain

performed by operators with minimal technical expertise (11). For the detection of PTB, a

of Xpert Ultra against culture to be 90.9% (8

gatifloxacin and ofloxacin), aminoglycosides (kanamycin, amikacin, capreomycin),

high mortality rates, and thus, its reduction may lead to reduced mortality (22). A larger 
proportion of people with true TB may receive effective therapy, and fewer individuals may 
be falsely diagnosed with the disease on clinical grounds alone, and incorrectly treated. Rapid 
detection of drug resistance may lead to more rapid initiation of effective treatment. These 
factors could potentially improve important patient outcomes.

blocks.title: Page 186
blocks.content:
Discussion 
Summary of findings 
This review assessed the impact of LC-aNAATs, LC-mNAATs and MC-aNAATs on patient 
outcomes in people being investigated for TB. We included two RCTs published between 2021 
and 2023 (one iRCT and one pragmatic cRCT) assessing the impact of Xpert Ultra, a type of 
LC-aNAAT (32, 33). Both studies involved adult participants.  
 
Data were available for two of the three secondary outcomes of interest and none for the 
two primary outcomes (all-cause mortality and cure). Time to diagnosis was reduced for 
those tested using Xpert Ultra compared to routine care (adj

summary.text: Discusses the findings of the review, which included two trials of Xpert Ultra in adults reporting secondary outcomes only, along with its strengths and limitation that no trials of other NAAT classes were found.

blocks.title: Page 187
blocks.content:
Implications for future research 
There is a need for high-quality trials that assess the impact of LC-aNAATs, LC-mNAATs and 
MC-aNAATs against relevant comparators on important patient outcomes to confidently 
inform policy decisions.  Studies included in this review were conducted within the WHO 
African region. Evidence from other WHO regions with high TB incidence such as South-East 
Asia and Western Pacific regions will help generalise findings on the impact of LC-aNAATs (38). 
Research on the impact of the three classes of NAATs on all-cause mortality and cure is 
needed. 
 
Conclusion

summary.text: Calls for high-quality trials of NAAT impact on patient outcomes, including outside the African region, and concludes that evidence that Xpert Ultra improves diagnosis and treatment times is limited.

Tuberculosis (TB) is one of the deadliest diseases with high mortality and morbidity. Globally, in 2022,

Report 2023). One of the major obstacles to the elimination of TB is the delay in accurate diagnosis.

Background 
The World Health Organization (WHO) estimated 1.3 million children (aged 0–14 years) were affected 
by tuberculosis (TB) in 2022. Globally, paediatric TB contributed to 16% of deaths among HIV-negative 
children in the same year. Multiple factors contribute to diagnostic delays and the consequent rise in 
incidence and mortality among children. The unique pathophysiology and clinical manifestations of 
TB in children make diagnosis particularly difficult. While there are practical difficulties in obtaining 
specimens for diagnosis, about 15% are positive on acid

We identified 2806 research articles for screening from searches of electronic sources and screened 
the titles and abstracts of 1138 unique articles. Of the 1138 articles, we excluded 988. We performed 
full-text screening of 151 articles. We included four studies for pulmonary TB and one of them for both 
pulmonary and extrapulmonary TB. Figure 1 shows the flow of studies through the screening and 
selection process.

reviews have traditionally assessed diagnostic accuracy of LC-a

5. DISCUSSION  
This systematic review summarizes the evidence on the parallel use of LC-aNAAT on respiratory

5.5 Strengths and weaknesses of the review  
This review represents the first estimations of incremental accuracy using parallel- compared to 
single-test strategies in children, based on comprehensive searching, strict inclusion, and 
standardized data extraction. For both review questions, sample sizes were large and comparative 
accuracy study analyses were based on a number of studies. We communicated extensively with the 
authors of the primary studies and were able to retrieve comprehensive data.

6. Author’s conclusions 
6.1 Implications for practice  
Almost half of the estimated tuberculosis cases in children and two-thirds among children less than 
5 years old are not reported to public health programs worldwide [World Health Organization 2023]. 
Underdiagnosis is the main contributor to this case detection gap, and leads to delays in treatment 
initiation [World Health Organization 2023]. As most children who die from tuberculosis never 
received treatment, there is a global need to increase detection of tuberculosis disease in children. 
Consequently, approaches and tools that inc

summary.text: Sets out the authors' conclusions on testing children for tuberculosis, stressing the large gap in case detection and the priority given to sensitivity over specificity. lack of data on the impact of parallel testing on patient outcomes for children with presumptive

1. BACKGROUND   
1.1 Target condition being diagnosed  
Tuberculosis remains a challenge to diagnose particularly in people with HIV. Diagnosis is often 
missed or delayed resulting in worse prognosis and patient outcomes. Globally, tuberculosis resulted 
in 1.1 million deaths among people without HIV and 167,000 deaths among people with HIV in 2022, 
and is the leading cause of death among people with HIV [Organization 2023].  
Tuberculosis predominantly affects the lungs as pulmonary tuberculosis, but can affect any part of 
the body, such as the lymph nodes, pleura, urogenital system, brain

isolation for detection of tuberculosis including Xpert MTB/RIF and Xpert Ultra assays (Cepheid, 
Sunnyvale, USA) for pulmonary tuberculosis [Zifodya 2021; Shapiro 2021] and extrapulmonary 
tuberculosis [Kohli 2021a] and urine LF-LAM for people with HIV [Bjerrum 2019c]. Some studies have 
found that urine LF-LAM and respiratory LC-aNAAT may be complementary for the diagnosis of 
tuberculosis disease in people with HIV [Shah 2014; Barr 2020; Lawn 2017b; Broger 2023a]. In the

1.3 Role of the tests 
The WHO operational handbook on tuberculosis states that “Urine LF-LAM should be used as an 
add-on to clinical judgement in combination with other tests. It should not be used as a replacement 
or triage test” [World Health Organization. 2021c]. For LC-aNAAT, the suggested role is an initial test 
replacing smear microscopy for the diagnosis of tuberculosis [World Health Organization. 2021a]. LF-
LAM and LC-aNAAT may be performed in parallel (i.e. LF-LAM in combination with LC-aNAAT) where 
a positive result on either test implies a positive result for the combination o

6. Author’s conclusions 
6.1 Implications for practice  
LC-aNAAT on respiratory sample is often the initial test to detect tuberculosis disease. Urine LF-LAM is 
an add on test that is in combination with clinical judgement and other tests (parallel use) for the 
diagnosis of HIV-associated tuberculosis. Respiratory LC-aNAAT and urine LF-LAM may be 
complementary when performed as part of a parallel testing strategy to diagnose all forms of HIV-
associated tuberculosis. Reasons for this observed increase in diagnostic sensitivity with addition of 
urine LF-LAM could be its ease of use, abilit

summary.text: Sets out the authors' conclusions for practice, describing respiratory LC-aNAAT as the usual first test and urine LF-LAM as a complementary add-on that can detect more HIV-associated tuberculosis, including in people unable to give sputum. It calls for implementation research on barriers and enablers that affect clinical decisions.

patient-important outcomes in children and in outpatient settings.

BACKGROUND 
 
In 2022, Tuberculosis (TB) was the second leading cause of death from a single infectious agent after 
COVID-19 globally(1).  TB resulted in 1.3 million deaths in 2022 with more than 10.6 million people who 
fell ill with TB, and of the 6.2 million people diagnosed with pulmonary TB worldwide, 63% were 
bacteriologically confirmed. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends using rapid molecular 
diagnostic tests as the initial diagnostic test in individuals with signs and symptoms of TB. Molecular-based 
testing offers rapid identification of the Mycobacterium tuberculos

summary.text: Gives background noting that TB caused 1.3 million deaths in 2022 and that WHO recommends rapid molecular tests as initial diagnostics. It explains that access remains limited in high-burden areas because of costs, infrastructure and staff shortages.

blocks.title: Page 383
blocks.content:
Low-complexity automated nucleic acid amplification tests (LC-aNAATs) are a class of TB diagnostics 
included in the mWRDs that can be used for TB diagnosis. They include Xpert® MTB/RIF (Xpert), Xpert® 
MTB/RIF Ultra (Ultra) (Cepheid, USA), and TrueNat™ (11). These tests provide initial detection of TB and 
resistance to rifampicin detection. 
 
Moderate complexity automated NAATs (MC-aNAATs) offer a high sample throughput for the initial 
detection of TB and resistance to rifampicin and isoniazid, providing more options for early diagnosis of 
TB and rifampicin-resistant TB but also addressin

summary.text: Describes the classes of NAATs, including Xpert, Xpert Ultra and Truenat, moderate-complexity automated tests and TB-LAMP. It notes that economic evidence for the newer tests is limited and has not been recently reviewed.

blocks.title: Page 384
blocks.content:
The overall aim of the present review is to identify, evaluate, and summarize the findings of available 
economic evidence on three classes of NAATs: 
• Low complexity automated nucleic acid amplification tests (LC-aNAATs) for TB 
diagnosis and detection of drug resistance.   
• Low-complexity manual NAAT (LC-mNAAT) TB-LAMP for TB diagnosis. 
• Moderate complexity automated NAATs (MC-aNAATs).  
 
2. 
METHODS 
 
This systematic review protocol has been developed according to the recommendations from the 
Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis Protocols (PRISMA-P) 2015

summary.text: States the review's aim of summarising economic evidence on three NAAT classes and begins describing the methods. It sets out inclusion criteria and excludes studies of active case-finding or triage before testing.

All people who screen positive, with signs and symptoms of TB, or with abnormal chest X-rays, people

3.1. Systematic review of LC aNAATs (Xpert, Ultra and TrueNat) 
 
Summary of Findings: 
A total of 1534 studies were identified in the original search, after removing duplicates, 736 potentially 
relevant studies were screened. Of these, 107 were assigned for full-text review and were evaluated 
against the inclusion and exclusion criteria, and 29 studies were included in the final systematic review 
(Figure 1). Of the 29 included studies, 22 (76%) assessed Xpert, six (21%) Ultra, and one study (3%) 
evaluated TrueNat. Ten of the studies evaluating Xpert were cost-effectiveness analyses, and 1

summary.text: Reports that 29 studies on LC-aNAATs were included from 1,534 records identified, and shows the PRISMA flow diagram with reasons for exclusion.

Quality assessment 
 
Two reviewers independently evaluated the reporting quality of each included study, and any 
disagreement was resolved by discussion. An 18-item modified Consolidated Health Economic Evaluation 
Reporting Standards (CHEERS) statement was used. The CHEERS statement is not a tool for assessing the 
quality of methods and does not provide an overall score. Instead, it assesses the quality of reporting. 
However, we estimated an overall score from the sum of items reported by each study compared to those 
indicated in the modified checklist. Each item that was met was rated a

summary.text: Describes quality assessment with an 18-item modified CHEERS checklist. It begins reporting cost-effectiveness results, including ICERs for Xpert and LAM strategies in hospitalized people with HIV.

blocks.title: Page 402

strategy for identifying more cases. 
 
Kaso & Hailu, 2021 compared Xpert to smear, and the ICER was $28 per additional case diagnosed (44). 
 
Cadavid et al., 2022 compared Xpert to smear and culture in adults & children and found Xpert to be more 
cost-effective with an ICER of $1017 compared to $1039 for culture (29).  
 
Hickey et al., 2022, compared one or two Xpert tests to smear and culture. One Xpert was found to be 
cost-saving at $6811 per patient (31).

3.2.  Systematic review of LC-mNAAT (TB-LAMP): 
 
3.2.1. Summary of Findings: 
After eliminating 638 duplicates, our search found 1,990 studies. Six studies were included in the final 
systematic review, as seen in Figure 2. Studies that did not involve people with TB, used LAMP as a 
diagnostic intervention, or did not contain cost data were excluded.  
 
Of the six included studies, one performed a cost-utility analysis (41), and two performed a cost-
affordability analysis (79,80). The three other studies (81–83) estimated the cost of TB-LAMP.

3.1.3. Economic Evidence Around LC-mNAAT (TB-LAMP): 
 
Diagnostic Cost per Sample:  
According to the costing studies, the cost per test ranged from $1 to $19 (all values in 2024 USD currency). 
The lowest cost of $1 did not provide any details on the cost calculation (81), while the second lowest cost 
of $2 included the cost of equipment, reagents, and consumables in a laboratory setting (82). The study 
integrated LAMP and Screen-printed graphene electrodes (SPGE). The TB-LAMP-EC components used in 
the study include LAMP, Redox probe, and SPGE, with various other components such as primers

summary.text: Reports that TB-LAMP costs per test ranged from $1 to $19, with the lowest estimates giving little or partial costing detail. It describes a Thai cost-utility study's methods, including direct medical and non-medical costs.

blocks.title: Page 423
blocks.content:
The conventional method, SSM followed by Culture/DST (Smear, Culture, and Sensitivity Testing), was 
established as the baseline for comparison. This approach incurred a cost of $212.90 and resulted in a 
QALY of 24.24. 
 
Next, the study evaluated alternative strategies: 
• 
SSM followed by TB-LAMP and DST costed $237.20 with a QALY of 25.02. The ICER was calculated 
to be $29.93 per additional QALY gained compared to the baseline. 
• 
TB-LAMP followed by DST costed $204.20 and a QALY of 25.17. 
• 
SSM followed by Xpert MTB/RIF incurred a higher cost of $277.60 but yielded a QALY of 24.77.

4. 
DISCUSSION 
 
LC-aNAAT discussion: 
Through a systematic review of published literature on LC aNAATs, we identified 29 studies that met our 
inclusion criteria. These included seventeen cost-effectiveness analyses and twelve cost analyses. Of the 
seventeen cost-effectiveness analyses, ten were on Xpert, six on Ultra and one on TrueNat. All twelve cost 
analyses were on Xpert. We did not find any cost analyses for Ultra or TrueNat.  
The studies included in our review were diverse, conducted across various settings and covered all income 
levels. This broad spectrum of research provides a

summary.text: Discusses the 29 LC-aNAAT studies, including 17 cost-effectiveness analyses and 12 cost analyses, all of the latter on Xpert. It contrasts this with an earlier review that found no Ultra studies and notes that only one Truenat study exists.

blocks.title: Page 432
blocks.content:
LC-nNAAT discussion: 
 
The present systematic review provides an in-depth analysis of the economic and cost-effectiveness of 
implementing TB-LAMP in diverse settings. Through a range of economic analyses, including cost-utility, 
cost-benefit, and cost-affordability assessments, this study contributes valuable insights into the potential 
role of TB-LAMP in tuberculosis diagnostics.  
 
The reviewed studies reveal that factors such as batch scenarios and larger settings influence the per-test 
costs, with the cost per test decreasing in specific scenarios. Testing volumes, location, and oper

summary.text: Discusses TB-LAMP evidence, noting that batch size and setting affect costs. It adds that a recent fall in TB-LAMP's price may improve its cost-effectiveness and affordability.

blocks.title: Page 433
blocks.content:
In conclusion, the collective findings suggest that TB-LAMP holds promise as a cost-effective and efficient 
diagnostic tool for tuberculosis when integrated into broader diagnostic algorithms, particularly in 
resource-constrained settings. The results of this study have important implications for policymakers and 
healthcare professionals involved in the diagnosis and management of tuberculosis. 
 
MC-aNAAT discussion: 
This systematic review is the first of its kind to investigate the economic aspects of using a new technology 
called MC-aNAATS for diagnosing drug-resistant tuberculosis (DR

summary.text: Concludes that TB-LAMP shows promise within diagnostic algorithms in resource-limited settings and that evidence on moderate-complexity NAATs is limited to one study. It begins the overall conclusion that Xpert was generally cost-effective compared with smear or culture.

blocks.title: Page 434
blocks.content:
heterogeneity in the cost-effectiveness results regarding Ultra, it was generally cost-effective compared 
to sputum smear microscopy.  TrueNat cost-effectiveness was reported in only one study but was found 
to be cost-effective compared to Xpert amongst children in India. In general LC aNAATs are likely to be 
cost-effective across a variety of settings when compared with SSM and/or culture. 
 
Few studies assessed parallel testing but when assessed parallel testing was the preferred strategy among 
PLHIV in South Africa using Ultra & LAM or Xpert & LAM compared with stand-alone testing. Fur

summary.text: Concludes that Ultra was generally cost-effective compared with smear and that Truenat was cost-effective in one study, so LC-aNAATs are likely cost-effective in many settings. The reference list then begins.

Executive Summary 
 
Background 
The WHO has introduced different classes of Nucleic Acid Amplification Tests (NAATs) depending on their 
infrastructure needs and mode of conduct. Latter NAATs are replacing standard Xpert MTB/RIF as initial 
diagnostic tests for Tuberculosis (TB) due to their high accuracy, rapid results and impact on patient 
important outcomes. Evidence on perspectives on the use, feasibility, acceptability and equity of newer 
NAATs in particular will inform an update to the WHO consolidated guidelines on TB diagnosis. 
Objectives 
To synthesize provider and end user

summary.text: Opens the executive summary of the qualitative synthesis, explaining that newer NAATs are replacing standard Xpert MTB/RIF as initial TB tests and that evidence on their feasibility, acceptability and equity will inform WHO guidelines. It states the objectives and notes that 49 qualitative studies were included, 17 from an updated search.

rest about Xpert MTB/RIF or rapid NAATs. The studies about Xpert Ultra were conducted in Africa and 
Eastern Europe and focused on all people with presumptive TB, drug resistant TB (DR-TB) and 
extrapulmonary TB (EPTB). All studies focused on perspectives about single tests and neither covered 
parallel testing nor moderate complexity NAATs. 
We identified 19 review findings from all included NAATs, nine of which were also about Xpert Ultra.  We 
grouped the findings into three overa

summary.text: Continues the executive summary, noting that included studies came from high TB burden settings in Africa, Asia and Eastern Europe, mostly on Xpert MTB/RIF, with two on Xpert Ultra and none on parallel testing or moderate-complexity NAATs. It summarizes 19 review findings grouped into what users value, related challenges and equity concerns, including Ultra's speed and accuracy but also infrastructure problems and fear of false results.

Concerns for access and equity 
Findings about Xpert MTB/RIF demonstrated concerns about sustainable funding, restrictions by donors, 
maintenance of the testing platforms, poor referral systems and dependence on outreach workers limiting 
access. Also protracted diagnostic delays, test underutilization, unavailability of community TB diagnostic 
facilities and too many eligibility restrictions limited access to testing. 
Similar to Xpert MTB/RIF, the reported concerns about equity for Xpert Ultra were its limited availability 
in health facilities, as well as high costs incurred by pat

summary.text: Summarizes access and equity concerns in the executive summary, such as funding, platform maintenance, referral weaknesses and costs. It concludes that qualitative evidence on newer NAATs is limited, that challenges mirror those of Xpert MTB/RIF, and recommends studies on parallel testing.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY 
 
Background 
The World Health Organization (WHO) estimates that in 2017, 10 million people became ill with TB 
globally. Drug-resistant TB is an enormous threat. In 2017, an estimated 558,000 people were newly 
diagnosed with rifampicin-resistant TB, 468,720 of whom had multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB). 
MDR-TB is caused by infection with M. tuberculosis bacteria that are resistant to at least rifampicin and 
isoniazid. The introduction and rollout of nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs) has revolutionized 
the area of TB diagnosis. WHO recommends Xpert, LPA,

summary.text: The opening of the executive summary for the review of moderate-complexity NAATs, giving the global TB and drug-resistant TB burden in 2017 and describing the review methods, including pooled meta-analysis in Stata.

blocks.title: Page 511
blocks.content:
506 
 
 
 
A total of 36 studies contributed to 39 unique datasets (four studies provided data for more than one 
index test). All the studies were performed in central laboratories as the index tests require sophisticated 
laboratory infrastructure. For most studies, samples were included in the study on arrival into the 
laboratory, as a result there was limited data on the demographics of the included patient population, 
such as age, HIV status, past TB history. 
 
A total of 29 studies with 13852 specimens (4767 TB positive specimens) provided data for evaluating 
TB detection from the fi

summary.text: Summarises the review results: 36 studies from central laboratories gave 39 datasets, with limited patient data, and the tests showed accuracy for TB, rifampicin and isoniazid resistance detection comparable to WHO-recommended molecular tests.

Background 
 
Tuberculosis (TB) is caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) bacteria. TB causes tremendous 
suffering worldwide and has surpassed HIV/AIDS as the world’s leading infectious cause of death. The 
World Health Organization (WHO) estimates that in 2017, 10 million people became ill with TB 
globally. Approximately, 1.3 million HIV-negative people and 300,000 HIV-positive people died from 
TB (WHO 2018). Drug-resistant TB is an enormous threat. In 2017, an estimated 558,000 people were 
newly diagnosed with rifampicin-resistant TB, 468,720 of whom had multidrug-resist

summary.text: Gives background on the TB and MDR-TB burden and on molecular tests already recommended by WHO, such as Xpert, line-probe assays, LAMP and Truenat.

blocks.title: Page 513
blocks.content:
508 
 
 
 
Recently, several companies have developed molecular tests for TB and RIF/INH resistance detection 
on centralized platforms, many of which have been established as multi-disease platforms, primarily for 
detection of Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), Human Papillomavirus (HPV) and Hepatitis C 
Virus. On these high-throughput platforms a large number of patient specimens can be tested in a shorter 
amount of time. Some assays can generate around 1000 results in just 8 hours (Cobas 8800 platform). 
This could help reduce the current problem of diagnostic delays and delay in treatme

summary.text: Describes high-throughput centralised molecular platforms for TB and resistance detection, such as Abbott RealTime and Roche Cobas, and the Bruker-Hain FluoroType assays with their extraction and detection systems.

blocks.title: Page 514
blocks.content:
509 
 
 
 
Becton Dickinson (BD) has developed a multiplexed real-time PCR (BD MAXTM MDR-TB, CE-marked 
since 2018) assay for the detection of Mtb and resistance to both RIF and INH. The platform utilizes 5- 
colour detection (UNITAID 2017). For Mtb detection, this assay detects multicopy genomic targets 
IS6110 and IS1081 as well as a single copy genomic target. For resistance, the assay detects rpoB, inhA 
promoter and katG genes. The LoD of BD Max MDR-TB assay has been reported as 0.5 cfu/ml for Mtb 
detection and 6 cfu/ml for resistance detection. The assay uses a fully-integrated, automat

summary.text: Describes the BD MAX MDR-TB assay and its genetic targets and detection limits, then sets out the review's eligible study types, including case-control studies and data from a WHO public call.

blocks.title: Page 515
blocks.content:
510 
 
 
 
Types of participants 
Patients of all age groups presumed of having or confirmed with pulmonary TB or MDR-TB, in all 
settings and all countries, were included. Specimen types were limited to pulmonary TB specimens (such 
as sputum, bronchoalveolar lavage, tracheal aspirate etc.). 
 
Index tests 
1. Abbott RealTime MTB and Abbott RealTime MTB RIF/INH 
2. Bruker-Hain FluoroType MTB and FluoroType MTBDR 
3. BD Max MDR-TB assay 
4. Roche Cobas MTB assay and Roche Cobas MTB RIF/INH assay 
 
 
Target conditions 
We considered the following three target conditions: resistance of Mtb to r

summary.text: Sets out the review's participants, the four index test families, the target conditions and the reference standards, including a composite standard combining phenotypic testing and sequencing.

The composite reference standard was constructed without knowledge of the index test results. 
 
Outcome measures 
 
For Mtb detection, sensitivity refers to the proportion of specimens or isolates with a culture positive 
for Mtb that were detected as Mtb-positive by the index test. 
For RIF- or INH-resistance detection, sensitivity refers to the proportion of specimens or isolates with 
the phenotypic or composite reference standard separately, demonstrating RIF/INH-resista

summary.text: Explains how discordant composite reference results were handled, defines sensitivity and specificity outcomes, and describes the search and screening by two review authors.

in one study, on the same or different specimens), it was considered as two or more datasets.

Meta-analysis was after pooling the dataset from all the index tests together. We also visually saw the 
results from each index test by forest plots. Bivariate random effects meta-analyses were performed (Chu 
2006; Reitsma 2005) using the metandi programme in Stata for index tests with enough studies that 
included data to calculate sensitivity, specificity, and 95% confidence intervals for each of these. 
Summary and individual estimates were also presented graphically with the 95% Confidence Interval 
(CI) interval and prediction region.

summary.text: Describes the bivariate random-effects meta-analysis methods in Stata, investigation of heterogeneity and the use of GRADE to assess certainty of evidence.

Summary of Findings tables. As recommended, we rated the quality of evidence as high (no points 
subtracted), moderate (one point subtracted), low (two points subtracted), or very low greater than two 
points subtracted) based on five factors: risk of bias, indirectness, inconsistency, imprecision, and other 
considerations. We subtracted one point when there was a serious issue identified or two points when 
there was a very serious issue identified in any of the factors used to judge the quality of evidence. Two 
review authors (MK and EM) discussed and applied the GRADE criteria.

Risk of bias 
 
Of the total 29 studies, 16 (55%) had high or unclear risk of bias as they either did prior testing before 
including specimens in the study or used convenience sampling or the method of participant selection 
was not reported. 
 
Applicability concern 
 
Only 45% of the studies were conducted in high TB/MDR TB burden country. 
 
Index test 
 
As all the index test assays were automated and thresholds were pre-defined, there is no scope of 
subjective interpretation of results. We judged all of them at low

Subgroup analysis: Smear status 
 
There were 26 studies that provided information for TB detection stratified by smear status. A total of 
2880 smear positive and 9447 smear negative specimens were evaluated. 
The sensitivity for smear positive specimens ranged from 93% to 100%. The pooled sensitivity was 
98.8% (93.7 to 99.7) (Table 2b) (Figure 4).

summary.text: A forest plot caption followed by the smear-positive subgroup analysis, with pooled sensitivity of 98.8%.

blocks.content: Forest plot (Figure 4) of sensitivity for TB detection in smear-positive specimens for 26 studies, listing TP, FP, FN and TN counts with sensitivity (95% CI) and a plot of each estimate on a 0–1 scale. Sensitivity ranges from 0.93 (Shaheed 2020) to 1.00, with most studies at 0.97 or above.

Forest plot (Figure 5) of sensitivity and specificity for TB detection in smear-negative specimens for 27 studies, listing TP, FP, FN and TN counts with sensitivity and specificity (95% CI) and plots of each estimate on a 0–1 scale. Studies are ordered by an 'S- C+' column (from 65.12 to 3.14); sensitivity varies widely, from 0.22 (Howlett 2020) to 1.00, while most specificity estimates are 0.91 or higher.

Meta-analysis of the data provided a pooled sensitivity of 86.1% (73.4 to 93.2) and the pooled specificity 
was 96.4% (93.6 to 98.0) (Table 2b) (Figure 5).

Sensitivity analysis: Manufacturer driven 
There were three studies which were manufacturer driven in this dataset for TB detection. We performed 
a sensitivity analysis excluding these studies driven by manufacturers to assess whether this would affect 
the results. We excluded Kostera 2016, Kostera 2018 and Paradis 2018. 
The pooled estimate for this sensitivity analysis for rifampicin was sensitivity of 97.6% (93.3 to 99.2), 
specificity of 98.6% (97.0 to 99.4). Similarly, for isoniazid the sensitivity and specificity was 85.7% 
(81.3 to 89.2) and 99.4% (98.6 to 99.7) respectively. Table 4

BACKGROUND 
 
In preparation for the upcoming guideline development group meeting “Nucleic acid amplification tests 
to detect TB and DR-TB” scheduled for 7-11 December, 2020, there is a need to summarize the current 
economic evidence on the following three classes of NAATs: 
 
1) Centralized assays that present end-to-end (E2E) solutions for detection of pulmonary TB 
and resistance to rifampicin and isoniazid; including the following commercially available 
platforms: Abbott RealTime MTB, Abbott RealTime RIF/INH, FluoroType MTB, 
FluoroType MTDBR, BD Max MDR-TB assay, Roche Cob

summary.text: Sets out the background to the economic evidence review, which summarizes cost data on three classes of nucleic acid amplification tests for TB and drug-resistant TB, starting with centralized end-to-end platforms such as Abbott RealTime, FluoroType, BD Max and Roche Cobas. It describes the database search strategy and its cost-related search terms.

blocks.title: Page 556
blocks.content:
551 
 
 
 
 
 
Due to limited direct evidence, several subsequent searches were performed in the same 4 databases as 
of late November to identify indirect evidence using these platforms in non-TB disease areas. Search 
strategies were run with the specific platform names but without the following search term for TB: 
(tuberculosis OR TB OR mycobacterium). Additional searches were also run with additional search terms 
for Genotype MTBDRsl and MTBDRplus to look for indirect evidence from line probe assays to inform  
the evidence around PZA LPA. 
 
Study selection & data extraction 
 
Studies

summary.text: Explains that because direct evidence was scarce, further searches looked for indirect cost evidence from the same platforms in other diseases and from line probe assays. It describes study selection and data extraction and an unpublished costing study that used time-and-motion observations in a South African laboratory to estimate unit test costs for BD Max and Hain.

In one-way sensitivity analyses, annual testing volumes were varied from <5,000 to >25,000 tests/year 
(Figure 3). Per-test cost was highly sensitive to testing volume when fewer than 5000 tests were 
conducted per year, but unit test costs begin to stabilize between 5,000 and 10,000 tests /year, and 
above 10,000 test per year, unit cost estimate was robust. When equipment can be multiplexed and 
used at capacity, per test cost can be minimized.

Additional literature searches conducted to l

summary.text: Reports that per-test cost was very sensitive to annual testing volume below 5000 tests and stabilized above about 10 000 tests. It notes that further searches found little additional data and that evidence on variation across sites and countries is limited.

No studies were identified that assessed cost-effectiveness analyses for any of the E2E solutions and 
extrapolation was not appropriate given differences in standard of care, different care cascades and 
associated costs, operational conditions, testing volume and diagnostic accuracy. Implementation 
considerations such as test placement, lab network, and ability of program to initiate treatment quickly 
will all likely impact unit test cost and cost-effectiveness. Economic modelling is needed across various 
settings to understand the range cost-effectiveness profiles of E2E sol

summary.text: States that no cost-effectiveness studies were found for the centralized end-to-end platforms and that extrapolating from other tests is not appropriate. It calls for economic modelling across settings and gives the same caution for the Xpert MTB/XDR test.

blocks.title: Page 561
blocks.content:
556 
 
 
 
 
Several factors that are likely influential on cost-effectiveness of Xpert MTB/XDR include diagnostic 
accuracy which may lead to more or fewer individuals being diagnosed compared with the standard of 
care, and this will vary by region depending on what the standard of care is across different regions. 
Along with diagnostic accuracy associated with the test itself, the diagnostic algorithm and placement of 
the Xpert MTB/XDR test within that algorithm has important implications as well. 
 
The novel Xpert MTB/XDR provides results in <90 minutes and therefore introduction of thi

summary.text: Discusses factors likely to shape the cost-effectiveness of Xpert MTB/XDR, including its accuracy relative to the local standard of care, its place in the diagnostic algorithm and its results in under 90 minutes. It notes that total costs and budget impact will depend on testing volume, XDR prevalence and current practice.

blocks.title: Page 562
blocks.content:
557 
 
 
 
 
 
Direct costs related to cartridge and machinery are provided from the manufacturer while several 
important items related to resource use including staff time, overhead and operational costs associated 
with implementing Xpert MTB/XDR have not been investigated. Differences in resource use between 
Xpert MTB/XDR and existing approaches will vary across settings using different phenotypic and 
genotypic DST. Important variability exists in costs of staff time and operational costs, such as testing 
volume across settings.

No cost-effectiveness studies were identified using the Genoscholar PZA-TB II. Extrapolation of cost- 
effectiveness data from other line probe assays is not advised due to differences in diagnostic accuracy, 
resistance prevalence, and the testing and treatment cascade of care. 
 
 
PRINCIPAL FINDINGS 
 
• 
Operational costs likely a large proportion of unit test costs and are largely unknown aside from 
equipment. These costs are also not always included in unit test costs making comparisons across 
estimates, methods and studies difficult. 
 
• 
Batch size and test volume are i

summary.text: States that no cost-effectiveness studies were found for the Genoscholar PZA-TB II assay and lists the review's principal findings. These stress that operational costs are largely unknown, that batch size and volume drive unit costs, and that budget impact depends on who is tested, resistance prevalence and current practice.

blocks.title: Page 565
blocks.content:
560 
 
 
 
 
the additional cost of treating more MDR and XDR patients in scenarios where sensitivity is improved, 
and more patients are initiating anti-TB treatment. 
 
Cost-effectiveness studies providing direct evidence were not identified and extrapolation is not 
advised. Cost-effectiveness may be impacted by changes in diagnostic accuracy, differences in standard 
of care across sites, diagnostic algorithm, reductions in turn-around-time among others. Without proper 
economic modelling, potential cost-effectiveness of various tests and testing approaches remains 
unknown. 
 
CONCLUSION

summary.text: Concludes that direct economic evidence on these new TB diagnostics is very limited and that cost-effectiveness and transmission modelling across settings is needed.

Background 
 
Description of the topic 
 
Tuberculosis (TB) causes 10 million cases and 1.5 million deaths annually and it is estimated that 3 million 
cases go undiagnosed each year (World Health Organization, 2020a). Drug-resistant TB (DR-TB) is a major 
threat to global TB control. Ending the global TB epidemic will be achievable over the next 20 years only 
if there is intensive action by all countries which have endorsed the End TB Strategy and its ambitious 
targets (World Health, 2015). Early diagnosis and prompt treatment of all persons of all ages with any form 
of drug-s

summary.text: Sets out the background to the qualitative review, noting TB's annual toll of 10 million cases and 1.5 million deaths, the threat of drug-resistant TB and the need for early diagnosis under the End TB Strategy. It explains that user perspectives on diagnostic technologies have rarely been studied and never systematically reviewed for a group of tests.

TB diagnosis is based on systematic reviews of diagnostic accuracy and cost-effectiveness. Accuracy 
studies do not reveal what users think of or experience with the diagnostic in question. Yet to understand 
why diagnostics are utilized, how effective they are and their impact on health equity, it is essential to 
answer questions around feasibility, added value and experiences which our review findings will provide.

This review focuses on users and potential users of automated NAATs of low complexity. Users include

officers who are involved in diagnosing and treating tuberculosis and drug resistant forms of TB as well as 
ordering, operating, maintaining diagnostics and acting on diagnostic test results. Potential users include 
users who do not (yet) utilize the diagnostic for instance because they are unable to access it or make it 
work within their routines or setting.

Results of the search 
 
We found 27 studies that met our inclusion criteria. We sampled 21 of these studies for inclusion in the 
analysis (see Figure 1: Flow chart Appendix 4). All of the sampled studies were published between 2012 
and 2020. Six studies remain to be reviewed which were not sampled as we assessed them as particularly

Discussion and conclusion 
This review synthesized qualitative research on user perspectives and experiences with automated NAATs 
of low complexity for detection of tuberculosis and tuberculosis drug resistance. We organized the 18 
individual review findings into the following three overarching categories: 
1) critical aspects users value: Patients value reaching diagnostic closure with an accurate diagnosis, 
avoiding delays, accessible facilities, keeping cost low. Healthcare professionals similarly value 
aspects of accuracy the resulting confidence in TB-NAAT results, rapid turnaround ti

summary.text: Summarizes the review's discussion, grouping its 18 findings into what users value, the challenges to achieving those values and the implications for access and equity. It recaps that patients value accurate, timely, affordable and accessible diagnosis, health professionals value accuracy, speed and drug-resistance information, and laboratory staff value improved working conditions. It calls for better implementation processes, including early inclusive stakeholder engagement, health system strengthening, better ground-level data and management of conflicts of interest.

summary.text: Opens Web Annex B.14, a 2020 interview study by Maastricht University researchers on user perspectives of NAATs for TB and drug-resistant TB, prepared for a WHO guideline meeting. It argues that user views on value, feasibility and acceptability matter alongside accuracy and that qualitative research can capture them. It describes the study's interviews with clinicians, laboratory staff, programme officers and patient advocates in Moldova, India and South Africa and the participant coding system.

blocks.title: Page 613
blocks.content:
Interviews were conducted over Zoom, Skype and phone. Topics discussed included: 1. current approach to 
diagnosing TB, MDR-TB, and XDR-TB including specific challenges; 2. experiences with using molecular 
TB diagnostics and the index tests specifically, including details on steps taken in the diagnostic process; 3. 
determining eligibility and treatment initiation as well as challenges and benefits of using the index tests; 4. 
overall usefulness of the index tests; 5. the feasibility of implementing the index tests; 6. their potential impact 
on health equity and; 7. how this relates to cur

It outlines the report's structure and introduces the first index test, low-complexity automated NAATs.

blocks.title: Page 614
blocks.content:
The first class of technologies to be evaluated at the WHO 2020 guideline meeting are low-complexity 
automated NAATs for the detection of resistance to isoniazid (INH) and second-line anti-TB medicines. One 
such test that we investigated in this study is the Xpert MTB/XDR cartridge by Cepheid. This particular 
cartridge detects mutations associated with resistance towards INH, fluoroquinolones (FLQ), second-line 
injectable drug (SLID) (amikacin, kanamycin, capreomycin) and ethionamide (ETH) (Cepheid, 2020). 
 
Benefits 
 
Although only three participants in this study had used the cartridge

summary.text: Describes the Xpert MTB/XDR cartridge, which detects resistance to isoniazid, fluoroquinolones, second-line injectables and ethionamide, and notes that few participants had used it. Participants anticipated benefits such as faster drug susceptibility results, earlier detection of isoniazid monoresistance and earlier information to guide treatment regimens.

hours. Because you would have RIF, you would have INH, you would have

from a patient”.

participant mentioned concerns regarding the size of the platform.

information on PZA resistance at more than one concent

Xpert® MTB/XDR Assay (Xpert MTB/XDR, Cepheid, Sunnyvale, USA) detects MTBC 
(Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex) DNA and genomic mutations associated with resistance to 
isoniazid, fluoroquinolones, ethionamide, and second-line injectable drugs (amikacin, kanamycin, 
capreomycin) in a single cartridge. Xpert MTB/XDR is intended for use as a reflex test in clinical 
specimens (unprocessed sputum or concentrated sputum sediments) already determined to be MTBC- 
positive. The test is included in a class of diagnostic technologies that are cartridge-based and of low 
complexit

summary.text: The executive summary of a systematic review of the Xpert MTB/XDR cartridge test, which detects tuberculosis and mutations linked to resistance to isoniazid, fluoroquinolones, ethionamide and second-line injectable drugs. BACKGROUND 
 
Early recognition and improved characterisation of tuberculosis drug resistance is a prerequisite for 
the rapid delivery of novel regimens to those who could benefit from them. For MDR/rifampicin- 
resistant-tuberculosis, the arrival of novel or repurposed drugs such as bedaquiline, clofazimine, and 
linezolid has revolutionized the efficacy of longer regimens, dispensing with the need for injectable 
drugs, and promising to deliver shorter all-oral regimens. Fluoroquinolones have an essential role and 
are also important for protecting second-line drugs like bedaquiline (WHO Co

summary.text: Gives background on the need for early detection of drug-resistant tuberculosis as new all-oral regimens emerge, noting the importance of fluoroquinolones and the gaps in culture-based drug susceptibility testing.

blocks.title: Page 635
blocks.content:

recommends that rapid techniques be used as the initial diagnostic tests to detect tuberculosis and 
rifampicin resistance in order to minimize delays in starting appropriate treatment (WHO 
Consolidated Guidelines (Module 3) 2020). The multiplexed nature of these new technologies 
theoretically permits susceptibility to be detected accurately and comprehensively for a single drug 
(where variants in multiple genes may cause resistance) and to several different drugs, each with their 
own sets of dist

summary.text: Notes that fewer than half of estimated drug-resistant TB cases are detected and explains WHO's support for rapid initial tests and the potential of multiplexed molecular assays. It describes the Xpert MTB/XDR assay and its claimed advantages, such as results in under 90 minutes on existing GeneXpert platforms.

states that “Specimens with “MTB Trace DETECTED” results when tested with the Xpert MTB/RIF 
Ultra Assay are expected to be below the limit of detection of the MTB/XDR Assay and are not

METHODS 
 
Types of studies 
We included cross-sectional studies and cohort studies that assessed the diagnostic accuracy of the 
index test. We included diagnostic accuracy studies in which cases and controls were sampled from a 
single source population (referred to as a single gate design). We excluded case-control studies where 
cases and controls were sampled from different populations (referred to as a two-gate design). The 
latter type of study is prone to bias, particularly when a study enrols participants with severe disease 
and healthy participants without disease (Rutjes 2005). We

summary.text: Describes the types of studies included, excluding two-gate case-control designs, along with participants, index test, target conditions and the phenotypic, genotypic and composite reference standards.

Mortality - we did not identify any studies that reported data for this outcome. 
Time to diagnosis - we did not identify any studies that reported data for this outcome. 
Time to start treatment - we did not identify any studies that reported data for this outcome. 
 
Search methods 
We searched the following databases: Ovid MEDLINE (OVID, 1946-present) and Embase (OVID, 
1947-present), for studies evaluating cartridge-ba

summary.text: Lists the review outcomes, noting that no studies reported cure, mortality or time to diagnosis or treatment, and describes the database searches, data extraction, quality assessment and meta-analysis methods.

BACKGROUND 
Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MTB) remains in the top 10 of causes for death globally, with an 
estimated 10 million cases and 1.2 million deaths globally in 2019.1 Of the 10 million cases, an 
estimated 465,000 were incident cases of multidrug resistant (MDR)/ rifampicin resistant (RR) 
tuberculosis, a marker for MDR-tuberculosis (TB).1

AUTHORS CONCLUSIONS 
The Nipro Genoscholar PZA TB assay appears to perform accurately to detect the presence of a wide 
range of different pncA variants. Majority of the studies conducted the assay using stored culture 
isolates; thus, we are unable to reach any conclusions regarding the use of the assay in clinical 
specimens. None of the studies stratified the results by resistance status, smear status or treatment 
outcome and so we are unable to reach any conclusions in this regard. 
 
IMPLICATIONS FOR RESEARCH 
This review suggests that the Nipro Genoscholar PZA TB assay is accurat

summary.text: Concludes that the Nipro GenoScholar PZA-TB assay appears accurate in detecting diverse pncA variants but evidence is mostly from stored isolates, and suggests using it as a reflex test after rifampicin resistance is detected.

Molecular diagnostic tests for drug susceptibility testing (DST) of Mycobacterium tuberculosis strains

only a few select drugs due to the limited number of mutations that can be probed. Some national

evidence supporting their use as an initial test of drug resistance is lower than that supporting their

summary.text: Concludes that the impact of targeted sequencing depends on where it is placed, with stronger evidence for reflex testing after rifampicin resistance is found than as an initial test, and calls for studies on extrapulmonary specimens.

blocks.title: Page 719
blocks.content:
Background  
 
Rapid, accurate detection of drug resistance for patients with tuberculosis is an important component 
within the process of ensuring optimal treatment outcomes both at an individual patient and 
population level. While empirical treatment with first line anti-tuberculosis drugs (isoniazid, 
rifampicin, ethambutol and pyrazinamide) would still result in successful outcomes for most patients 
in the world, this approach has become increasingly hazardous in some countries over the past 
decades.(1) Offering patients treatment regimens containing too few efficacious drugs risks 
tr

summary.text: Sets out the background to a WHO-commissioned review of targeted next-generation sequencing (tNGS) for detecting drug resistance in tuberculosis, explaining that empirical treatment risks failure and amplified resistance where resistance is common. It notes that phenotypic drug susceptibility testing remains out of reach for most patients and that molecular tests such as Xpert MTB/RIF, line-probe assays and Xpert XDR cover only some drugs. It argues that new regimens such as BPaLM have outpaced companion diagnostics and that sequencing directly from samples could help protect these drugs.

Clinical pathway 
 
The analyses presented here first assess the diagnostic accuracy of tNGS assays for DST for 
isoniazid, rifampicin, ethambutol, pyrazinamide and fluoroquinolones (levofloxacin and moxifloxacin) 
among all patients diagnosed with TB and then assess the diagnostic accuracy for all covered drugs 
(except rifampicin) for patients whose strains have already been identified as resistant to rifampicin 
by Xpert MTB/RIF® or Xpert Ultra®. Further sub-group analyses examine the performance by semi-
quantitative Xpert MTB/RIF® or Xpert Ultra®  esult (‘ e y lo ’ o  ‘lo ’ co pa e  to ‘

It explains the four possible test outcomes, true and false positives and negatives, and their consequences for patient treatment. It also notes that Deeplex Myc-TB can report uncharacterized mutations, which the review counts with failures as indeterminate results; some quoted terms on the page have missing letters in the extracted text.

Methods 
 
Types of studies and participants 
 
Data were included from both published and unpublished, prospective, observational clinical studies 
of tNGS platform diagnostic accuracy. We included all studies where tNGS had been performed 
directly from clinical samples and excluded studies where tNGS had been performed exclusively on 
cultured isolates. We included all samples as long as data on tNGS result and reference had been 
finalized and were not subject to change. All studies were required to have comparator pDST data 
as a reference, and for rifampicin, ethambutol and pyrazinamide

countries. Sensitivity for the flouroquinolones was 94%-96%, which is com

blocks.title: Page 772
blocks.content:
Background: Tuberculosis (TB) remains one of the leading causes of morbidity and mortality 
globally. Our review aims to summarize the current economic evidence around using targeted Next 
Generation Sequencing (tNGS) for the diagnosis of DR-TB. 
Methods: We conducted a systematic review on the economic evaluation of using either tNGS or 
WGS to diagnose DR-TB. The following three databases were used: PubMed, EMBASE and 
SCOPUS. The search was run on October 30, 2022. We did not restrict by year of publication; age 
group; country; income-level; comparator group; HIV status, or other comorbidi

summary.text: Summarises the economic review, which searched three databases in 2022 and included ten studies on tNGS and whole genome sequencing for drug-resistant TB, finding tNGS costs of about US$70 per sample and wider ranges for whole genome sequencing. It identifies sequencing as the costliest step, reagents and consumables as the main cost components and drivers such as sequencer choice, coverage depth and batching, and calls for more cost-effectiveness research.

blocks.title: Page 773
blocks.content:
1. INTRODUCTION  
 
Tuberculosis remains one of the leading causes of morbidity and mortality globally (1). In 2021, the 
World Health Organization (WHO) estimated approximately 10.6 million new cases of TB 
occurred, and over 1.6 million deaths, the latter being an increase in mortality compared to trends 
seen between 2005 and 2019 (2, 3). DR-TB was first recognized in the late 1940s and has become 
an increasing public health concern (2). DR-TB can be further classified as Rifampin-resistant TB 
(RR-TB), Isoniazid-resistant TB (IR-TB), Multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB), Pre-extensively 
Drug-

summary.text: Introduces the economic review, citing WHO estimates of 10.6 million TB cases and 1.6 million deaths in 2021 and defining forms of drug-resistant TB from rifampicin-resistant to extensively drug-resistant. It notes that resistance is concentrated in some high-burden countries and regions. It then explains that conventional phenotypic testing is slow and needs high-level biosafety laboratories and skilled staff.

Alternative second-line diagnostic approaches for DR include Line Probe Assays (LPAs), which 
avoid many of the steps in conventional pDST (19). This is another type of probe-based molecular 
test. In 2008, the WHO approved the use of LPAs for the diagnosis of MDR-TB, and there are 
currently ten different types commercially available (19, 20). Most LPAs can only diagnose 
rifampin resistance via the rpoB gene, and/or isoniazid resistance via the katG gene; but newer 
modalities can also detect resistance in

It then begins the methods, noting the review followed PRISMA guidelines with a librarian-supported search strategy.

It lists the databases searched in October 2022, the inclusion of studies on confirmed or suspected DR-TB, and the cost outcomes of interest such as cost per sample, component costs, costs per step and ICERs.

2.4. Statistical Analysis  
Due to the limited number of studies available and the high degree of methodological heterogeneity 
between studies, a meta-analysis was deemed not appropriate. Instead, a narrative summary review 
was performed. 
 
All cost data was inflated to 2021 in local currency and converted to 2021 USD using the relevant 
International Monetary Fund (IMF) exchange rates and inflation index (36). We contacted study 
authors for missing or unclear data.  
 
2.5. Assessing the Quality of Evidence  
We used a modified version of the Consolidated Health Economic Evaluation Report

summary.text: Explains that heterogeneity ruled out meta-analysis, so a narrative synthesis was done with costs converted to 2021 US dollars, and that study quality was rated with a modified CHEERS checklist. It then describes which cost measures the included tNGS and WGS studies reported and notes that few costed the phenotypic comparator.

blocks.title: Page 777
blocks.content:
3.1.1. Economic Evidence Around tNGS 
3.1.1.1. Summary of Findings 
Six studies reported on costs for tNGS approaches (Table 1). Three of the studies were performed in 
the US, one collected specimen from both Ethiopia and Hong Kong, one in the UK, and one in 
Moldova with year of cost valuation ranging from 2018-2021 (Table 1). Of the tNGS studies, two 
used on-site testing, and four required sample transport to a central lab for processing (Table 1). We 
identified two studies that assessed diagnostic cost per sample for tNGS, and one that assessed this 
for pDST as a diagnostic comparator.

summary.text: Summarizes six studies reporting tNGS costs for drug-resistant TB, their settings and whether testing was on site or centralized. It reports the limited data on cost per sample and the wide range in sequencer prices, from about $1 000 for a Nanopore MinION to over $200 000 for an Illumina NextSeq.

blocks.content:

with the lowest being Illumina MiSeq100, and the highest Nanopore MinION. However, this was 
based on limited data (n=1). The per sample cost for reagents and consumables was found to be as 
low as $6.20 for MiSeq and $15.32 for iSeq100 (Table 7B). For this determination, samples had 
15,000-fold coverage, which account for 99% of the genome, and a 30x-fold depth of coverage. For 
Chan et al. (2020), with Nanopore MinION, reagents and consumables were as high as $67.02 per 
sample per 24-plex work

4. DISCUSSION  
4.1. Interpretation of Systematic Review Findings 
To the best of our knowledge, this systematic review is the first of its kind to look at the economic 
evidence around using tNGS for the diagnosis of DR-TB. tNGS is a relatively new technology, and 
despite broad inclusion criteria, only ten suitable articles were found. There were no manuscripts 
with direct comparisons

summary.text: Gives quality scores for the scoping review studies and opens the discussion, describing the systematic review as the first on tNGS economics for drug-resistant TB and noting the scarcity of data. It discusses why per-sample costs vary, including platform choice, coverage depth and early-run inefficiencies reported in one study.

blocks.title: Page 782
blocks.content:
Lastly, lower sample volumes and less batching per run are likely to be associated with a greater 
costs per sample. This includes batching across TB samples or multiplexing with different 
organisms. While not explicitly mentioned in any of the papers, this could likely impact costs by 
spreading out certain overhead (e.g., labor costs) or equipment costs (e.g., sequencer flow cell) 
among more samples. This latter impact was discussed with the authors of one of the included 
manuscripts (41).

It then interprets the scoping review, highlighting a modelling study in which molecular testing plus WGS was the most cost-effective TB diagnostic strategy owing to greater sensitivity and faster diagnosis.

blocks.title: Page 783
blocks.content:
5. CONCLUSION 
 
Given the growing interest in tNGS as a diagnostic modality, there are a number of additional data 
points that would be helpful to characterize. First, further studies are needed to determine additional 
economic markers, such as cost-effectiveness analyses or ICERs. Second, it will be prudent to 
develop a better understanding of the various factors that may impact cost, such as the impact of 
batching and multiplexing, as well as country-dependent factors. Lastly, it would be helpful to have 
more data points that include all relevant costs, such as overhead, total lab equi

summary.text: Concludes that more research is needed on cost-effectiveness, cost drivers such as batching and multiplexing, and full costing including overheads before tNGS and WGS economics for drug-resistant TB are well understood. It introduces the PRISMA flow diagram for the systematic review.

blocks.content:
Abstract 
 
 
BACKGROUND 
Timely drug resistance detection is essential to global tuberculosis management. Novel molecular 
testing tools are being developed to rapidly detect multi-drug resistant Tuberculosis (MDR-TB) which is 
needed for more effective and timely treatment of MDR-TB. Targeted next generation sequencing 
(tNGS), is new molecular-based rapid diagnostic technology (used on a sputum sample), that can 
provide comprehensive diagnosis of MDR-TB in a short turnaround time of a few days, compared to the 
standard culture-based phenotypic MDR-TB diagnostics that take multiple weeks.

summary.text: The abstract explains that tNGS on sputum can diagnose drug-resistant TB within days instead of weeks, but faces implementation barriers. It states that interviews with implementers aimed to inform a new WHO guideline by exploring acceptability, feasibility, values, preferences and equity. It begins reporting that implementers saw the technology as a major advance but found platforms complex, with few chances to catch errors early.

scientists are needed to perform the tests. In these LMIC settings, such specialized  laboratory 
infrastructure and staff may only be available at centralized laboratories and not necessarily at 
regional laboratories.

It also notes supply chain delays and data management concerns. Turning to values and equity, participants worried about the cost of equipment, reagents and maintenance and called for comprehensive costing.

It concludes that adoption in low- and middle-income countries should weigh ease of use, organizational context and stakeholder values as well as effectiveness.

blocks.title: Page 827
blocks.content:
Background 
 
Tuberculosis (TB) remains a major global public health threat. One of the most challenging forms of the 
disease is multidrug resistant TB (MDR-TB), due to higher morbidity and mortality, complexity of 
treatment and higher cost (1). WHO estimated that in 2016, close to half a million people were 
diagnosed with MDR-TB (2). It is estimated that only two out of every three patients with MDR-TB are 
diagnosed, of those diagnosed, only three out of four are treated, and only half of those treated are 
cured. This results in the majority (75%) of patients with MDR-TB not being cured;

summary.text: Gives background on MDR-TB, noting that only about two in three cases are diagnosed and most patients are not cured, partly because of diagnostic and treatment delays. It explains that culture-based drug susceptibility testing takes weeks and that the End TB Strategy calls for universal testing. It then describes the tNGS workflow, stressing the precise library preparation needed before sequencing.

blocks.content: A linear workflow diagram of targeted next-generation sequencing (tNGS) with four steps joined by arrows: DNA extraction, library preparation, sequencing and data analysis.

blocks.title: Page 828
blocks.content:

generation and data storage (5).  
Figure 1: tNGS workflow 
 
Targeted tNGS therefore hold the potential, especially in high-burden TB settings, for effective 
treatment and control of the spread of MDR-TB, but there are obstacles to the uptake of novel, rapid 
technologies. Obstacles to similar rapid diagnostics have been documented and include concerns 
about costs, integration into existing laboratory workflows, technical training and skill requirements for 
utilization of the technology,

summary.text: Completes the description of the tNGS workflow and notes known barriers to rapid diagnostics, such as cost, workflow integration, training and interpreting sequence data. It explains why health worker perspectives on implementability matter. It restates the study's objective of informing WHO guidance on tNGS.

blocks.title: Page 829
blocks.content:
Methods 
 
Study design 
This was a cross-sectional observational qualitative study using semi-structured interviews. 
 
Setting 
The main stakeholders were implementers of the FIND trial in the main reference laboratories that 
implemented the tNGS trial, located in Georgia, India, and South Africa.   
 
Participants  
We were interested to learn about how the experiences and perceptions of the stakeholders who were 
involved with implementing the FIND trial in the three countries. Participant selection was therefore 
purposive and representative; purposive as the aim was to include in-countr

summary.text: Describes the qualitative methods, using semi-structured interviews with implementers of the FIND trial in reference laboratories in Georgia, India and South Africa, plus coordinators and other global sites. It explains purposive selection of staff with hands-on experience. It also describes recording, verbatim quotes and interview summaries as the main data source.

It notes confidentiality agreements, so countries are anonymized as A, B and C. Findings begin with strong acceptability because tNGS is comprehensive, uses sputum and is fast.

Feasibility considerations of tNGS technology 
 
The overall sentiment was that the tNGS technology needs to be further developed before it can be 
considered  fully ready for operational use. Implementers experienced a range of challenges with 
implementing the tNGS technology which influenced their views on the feasibility of the technology

It lists challenges such as start-up problems, specialized staff and laboratories, supply chains, complex library preparation, data management and security, and the need to keep the WHO mutation catalogue updated. It begins describing how skilled molecular scientists were available only at central laboratories.

Reports differed in the level of detail they provided, and reports were presented in a format that could 
be used for clinical decision-making. For each drug, information on resistance is expressed in terms of 
whether there is resistance or susceptibility to the drug, and the confidence level of that test result

Participants noted uncertainty about resistance to newer drugs such as bedaquiline. They called the WHO catalogue essential and wanted automatic links between tNGS software and laboratory information systems.

blocks.title: Page 837
blocks.content:
Differences on feasibility views across different tNGS platforms 
 
The overall sentiment that is that all three the tNGS platforms need to be further developed before it is 
fully ready for operational use. However, there were differences in the sentiments about feasibility 
challenges, with some being regarded as having more substantial challenges. The high level of 
technical complexity of the sample preparation stages (mainly the library preparation stage) was 
considered a key challenge for the Deeplex platform. Sample preparation prior to sequencing was 
considered less of a challenge fo

summary.text: Compares feasibility views across platforms, with library preparation seen as more complex for Deeplex than for Oxford Nanopore. Both were thought to lack early error detection, risking wasted runs. Quotes describe the products as immature and not yet market-ready.

blocks.title: Page 838
blocks.content:
Areas of concern that would need to be addressed in future development of the tNGS platform include 
the need to reduce the level of complexity of the sequencing procedures and develop more automated 
interlinkage with the data analysis processes. Mechanisms would need to be in place to ensure a 
continuous supply of specialist products, especially the reagents. Local vendors are needed for the 
maintenance of equipment and to provide technical support.  
 
A lower complexity tNGS platform is needed to decentralize the use of tNGS technology: A key 
concern was the high level of complexity of

summary.text: Lists areas for future tNGS development, such as reducing complexity, automating links to data analysis, securing supplies and local technical support. Participants wanted a lower-complexity platform, for example with robotic liquid handling, so testing could be decentralized. Some hoped for point-of-care tests close to patients.
