(Country C, participant 1). 
 
Equitable access 
 
Centralized, reference laboratory placement requires tradeoffs in terms of equitable access:  
Stakeholders agreed given the complexity of tNGS technology (and the specialist laboratory and HR 
requirements), it is only suitable for placement at centralized, reference laboratories that can perform 
molecular testing. This has equity considerations as it may mean less access for some regions of the 
country without reference laboratorys. The MDR

summary.text: Discusses equitable access, noting that placing tNGS only in reference laboratories may disadvantage some regions and that batching in low-caseload settings causes delays. A participant called for 'plug and play' single-sample testing at affordable cost. It begins listing the costs that comprehensive costing should include, such as computing and storage.

associated with securing high internet capacity and interlinking the tNGS information platform and the 
laboratory’s own information system.  
 
Cost effectiveness should include test effectiveness and impact on TB treatment outcomes: While 
there is appreciation for dramatic improvements in scope and turnaround time of diagnosis of MDR 
TB, the real value should be measured in terms of the accuracy of the test and the impact on TB 
treatment outcome. Test results should be accurate and valid, and t

summary.text: Adds that costing should include maintenance, internet capacity and links to laboratory information systems. Participants argued cost-effectiveness should reflect accuracy, indeterminate results and impact on treatment outcomes, accepting short delays for reliable results. A participant hoped tNGS would replace rather than add to existing tests.

would fit with a transition from phenotypic testing towards genotypic testing; how phenotypic testing 
may still be needed in future scenarios. And costing of the use of tNGS should include the costs of the 
scenario where both genotypic and phenotypic testing for MDR TB would still be required.

purpose of the rapid diagnostic in the overall cascade and the need for it to be easily implemented:

Abstract 
 
BACKGROUND 
Timely drug resistance detection is essential to global tuberculosis management. Novel molecular 
testing tools are being developed to rapidly detect multi-drug resistant Tuberculosis (MDR-TB) which is 
needed for more effective and timely treatment of MDR-TB. Targeted next generation sequencing 
(tNGS), is new molecular-based rapid diagnostic technology (used on a sputum sample), that can 
provide comprehensive diagnosis of MDR-TB in a short turnaround time of a few days, compared to the 
standard culture-based phenotypic MDR-TB diagnostics that take multiple weeks. Th

summary.text: The abstract of the qualitative evidence synthesis, explaining that tNGS can give comprehensive drug-resistance results within days but faces technical, organizational and economic barriers. It describes a rapid review that searched Medline and other sources in 2022, with single-reviewer screening and planned thematic synthesis and CERQual assessment. It reports that no eligible studies were found and points to the companion primary study and a 2022 Cochrane review of other rapid TB tests as indirect evidence.

deserves more attention.

A rapid review of qualitative evidence on the experiences and perceptions of  tNGS technology for

This study seeks to provide evidence to inform the new WHO guideline for use of tNGS technology for 
MDR-TB diagnostics. The objective is to identify and synthesize qualitative evidence on 
implementation considerations of tNGS technology for MDR-TB, related to acceptability, feasibility, 
values and preferences and equity, from the perspectives of health workers as implementers.

streamlining methods used for systematic reviews (16). Rapid review techn

Electronic searches  
We used a combination of a systematic search strategy and an open searching approach. The search 
strategy used a set of search terms associated with NGS technology as an intervention, with MDR-TB 
and qualitative research (and associated names). We searched Medline with no year or language 
limits.  We designed a search strategy and ran on Aug 19, 2022, and  rerun on Oct 10, to include WGS

search  with open searching on Google

It reports that no eligible studies were found, mostly because papers were quantitative, discussion pieces or based on hypothetical views.

blocks.title: Page 859
blocks.content:
Discussion and recommendations 
 
The aim of this study was to identify and synthesize qualitative evidence on implementation 
considerations of the new tNGS technology for diagnosing multi-drug resistance TB, to inform the new 
WHO guideline on rapid TB diagnostics. This review did not yield any direct evidence from primary 
qualitative perception studies on tNGS technology as no studies could be found.  
 
Research and practice implications 
Given this is an empty review, there are clearly research gaps waiting to be filled. While there are 
several studies testing the accuracy of tNGS techn

summary.text: Discusses the empty review, noting that tNGS is not yet widely operational and that future effectiveness studies offer chances to study implementers' experiences. It recommends including qualitative process evaluations and draws on a Cochrane review of other rapid TB diagnostics that highlights implementation factors. It also notes that patients' experiences of rapid TB diagnostics are understudied.

blocks.title: Page 860
blocks.content:
Strength and limitations  
The QES found no eligible studies most likely due the newness of the tNGS technology. We anticipated 
finding very little information, and a pilot search prior to embarking on the review may have confirmed 
the lack of information. The value of having conducted the review and coming up empty, it that it 
confirms there is gap in qualitative studies on implementation of TNGS for MDR-TB. This knowledge is 
useful to encourage researchers to include qualitative and or mixed method process evaluations 
alongside future operational research on tNGS technology.

summary.text: Discusses strengths and limitations, noting that the empty result confirms a research gap and that the review used multiple search methods but rapid-review shortcuts such as single-reviewer screening. It closes with acknowledgements and a statement of no conflicts of interest.

The quality of studies evaluating Diaskintest performance was difficult to assess due to 
inconsistencies and incomplete reporting of study methods and sample recruitment. This resulted in 
several “unknown” assessments against the quality criteria. Of the 16 studies evaluating the 
sensitivity of Diaskintest, risk of bias was high in 5 (31.3%) studies where test assessors were not 
blinded to TB culture results,34 46 49 51 53 and unclear in  at least one of the four risk of bias criteria in

summary.text: Describes risk of bias in the included studies, noting that poor reporting left many quality criteria unclear and that many Diaskintest studies lacked blinding to culture or comparator results. Executive summary 
 
Background 
The diagnostic tests in current use for identification of TB infection are the tuberculin skin test (TST) 
and interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA). The safety of TST, an in-vivo test, is well established and 
associated with only uncommon adverse reactions. Over the last decade, novel skin-based tests for 
TB infection using TB specific antigens (TBST) have been developed. Evidence on the safety of these 
tests has not been systematically reviewed. 
 
Method 
We systematically searched for studies reporting the outcomes of our interest: local reactions

summary.text: The executive summary of the safety review explains that the tuberculin skin test is known to be safe but that newer antigen-based skin tests had not been systematically assessed. It describes searches of English, Russian and Chinese databases up to July 2021, plus manufacturer data and a WHO call for data. It notes that some studies were at high risk of bias owing to lack of blinding or passive collection of adverse events.

blocks.title: Page 921
blocks.content:
58 
 
 
The pooled risk of any injection site reaction (ISR) due to C-Tb (N= 2931, 5 studies) was not 
significantly different from TST (RR 1.05; 95%CI 0.70-1.58). Over 95% of ISR were reported as mild or 
moderate; common ISR included pain, itching and rash. In one study that allowed, 49/153 (37.6%) of 
participants given C-Tb developed any systemic adverse events (e.g. fever and headache) in 
comparison with 37.6% (56/149) in those given TST (RR 0.85 95%CI 0.6-1.2). The remaining studies 
did not allow the comparison of systemic adverse events. 
 
In a single paper in China reporting combine

summary.text: Summarises key findings: injection site reactions with C-Tb were no more common than with TST and were mostly mild or moderate, while one Chinese report found more reactions with C-TST. Diaskintest safety data were too inconsistent to pool, and overall no safety signal was seen that would affect the choice between the novel tests and TST. The background notes that about a quarter of the world's population has tuberculosis infection.

distinguish between active TB disease and TB infection, nor are they useful predictors of progression 
to active disease.5 More accurate diagnostic tests are critical to the achievement of the targets of 
End TB Strategy.6

reactions, although systemic reactions like headache, fever and even lymphadenitis have also been 
reported.11 12  Induration/swelling/inflammation are the intent of the skin tests and may not 
necessarily be “adverse” reactions in all instances, however some clinical trials consider these as

Study Screening and Data Collection Process: 
In support of data synthesis for the GDG, we developed a broad search strategy for English papers to 
allow title and abstract screening informing multiple systematic reviews addressing other objectives.  
The initial list of English titles and abstracts were reviewed by two independent reviewers (YH and 
LEZ) to identify studies reporting any new skin tests regardless of the outcomes of interest. This was 
followed by screening of titles and abstracts by two independent reviewers (YH and IK) and 
screening of full-text articles. Two Russian

summary.text: Describes how studies in English, Russian and Chinese were screened and data extracted by pairs of independent reviewers, with disagreements resolved by discussion. It explains how risk of bias was judged for randomised and non-randomised studies.

Injection site reactions 
For C-Tb, the frequency of any ISR reactions ranged from 23.7% to 53.1% (Table 4). Most 
(>95%) ISR were reported as mild to moderate by the investigators (mild: easily tolerated; 
moderate: sufficient to interfere with daily activities; severe: sufficient to prevent normal 
activity). Common ISR included itching, pain, and rash. One study reported only mild 
reactions and in four studies, <5% were of severe intensity. The pooled RR did not show 
evidence of a significant difference in the frequency of any ISR between C-Tb and TST 
(Figure 2, Figure A1).  Howe

blocks.title: Page 958
blocks.content:
BACKGROUND 
 
With an estimated 1.7 billion people infected with tuberculosis infection (TBI), progression of infection to 
active TB disease poses a large public health risk1. Prominent risk factors of this transition include clinical risk 
factors such as human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), diabetes, undernutrition, and contextual or societal risk 
factors in the most vulnerable and disadvantaged populations including, TB case contacts especially children, 
immigrants2. WHO recommends TB preventive treatment (TPT) to disrupt disease progression. Testing for TB 
infection is recommended to gu

summary.text: Gives the background to the review, noting about 1.7 billion people with TB infection and WHO's recommendation of preventive treatment guided by testing where possible. It contrasts the tuberculin skin test, which needs two visits and is less specific after BCG vaccination, with blood-based IGRA tests, and introduces newer specific skin tests.

blocks.title: Page 959
blocks.content:
sensitivity for TBI, especially in resource-constrained settings and contexts where BCG vaccination is 
implemented routinely. 8,9. The diagnostic accuracy of the tests alone, however, is not sufficient evidence for 
the recommendation of their use in TBI testing guidelines. To provide sufficient evidence for the intervention, 
cost-effectiveness must also be considered to ensure that the tests are affordable and feasible to implement.  
 
The present report provides a systematic review of the literature on the cost-effectiveness of the new tests 
compared to currently available tests for TBI.

summary.text: Explains that accuracy alone does not justify recommending the new skin tests, so their cost-effectiveness must be examined. It states the research question and four objectives: two systematic reviews of costs and cost-effectiveness of the new and current tests, and modelling of cost-effectiveness across settings.

Systematic literature reviews  
 
Abstract 
Background: The tuberculin skin test (TST) and interferon-gamma release assays (IGRA) are the currently used 
tests for identifying individuals with TB infection that should be offered TB preventive treatment, however 
challenges around access and implementation have limited their use. Novel Mycobacterium tuberculosis 
specific skin tests (TBST) such as the DiaskinTest, ESAT6-CFP10 (now called C-TST) C-Tb, and DPPD have been 
developed in recent years, these may provide accurate and scalable options. We conducted a systematic 
review of the economic

summary.text: The abstract of the systematic reviews, explaining that novel TB-specific skin tests may offer accurate, scalable alternatives to the tuberculin skin test and IGRA. It reports finding only eight economic studies of the new tests, seven on Diaskintest in Russia and one in Brazil, with low unit costs but generally poor study quality, and calls for more high-quality studies.

blocks.title: Page 962
blocks.content:
Methods 
 
We performed two different literature reviews. 
(a) a primary review looking at the costs and cost-effectiveness of the novel skin tests (registered on 
PROSPERO: CRD42021275585) 
(b) a secondary review for the cost-effectiveness of PPD-TST and IGRAs tests (registered on PROSPERO: 
CRD42021275684) 
 
Firstly, we reviewed the literature on the cost and cost-effectiveness of the novel tests. Due to the anticipated 
lack of evidence, a secondary review of the literature surrounding the cost and cost- effectiveness of the standard 
PPD-TST and IGRA was also conducted to supplement the p

summary.text: Describes the methods of two registered literature reviews, one on costs and cost-effectiveness of the new skin tests and a secondary one on the tuberculin skin test and IGRA. It lists the English, Chinese and Russian databases searched, the three concept groups of search terms, and the use of manufacturer data and a WHO public call for data.

blocks.title: Page 963
blocks.content:
We did not have an exclusion criterion for specific populations, and all articles had to be published in English, 
Chinese or Russian and relate to TBI in humans. Papers had to be full original economic evaluations, meaning 
having clear measures of costs, outcomes, and sufficient incremental analysis using the healthcare perspective. 
No time restriction was imposed for the primary review on novel skin tests, whereas we searched those articles 
published between 2011 to July 2021 for the secondary review on PPD-TST or IGRA tests. 
 
Study selection & data extraction 
Studies were included if

summary.text: Sets out inclusion criteria requiring full economic evaluations from a health care perspective, published in English, Chinese or Russian, and the test products covered. It describes how reviewers screened papers in each language, extracted data, converted costs to 2021 US dollars and assessed quality with the Drummond checklist.

chosen for full-text screening and 29 papers were selected for analysis (see PRISMA flow in F

Description of the articles found in the primary review (specific TBST)  
 
Eight economic evaluations were conducted from middle-income countries (Russia and Brazil), these mostly 
compared DiaskinTest against PPD-TST (Table A2, supplementary). One study met most of the Drummond’s 
checklist factors and reported all the required information. Steffen et al (2020) 12 studied the cost-effectiveness 
of two novel TBST (Diaskintest and C-TST) for people living with HIV (PLHIV) in Brazil compared to PPD-TST and

summary.text: Figure 2, a PRISMA flowchart for the secondary review of the tuberculin skin test and IGRA, followed by a description of the eight studies on the new tests, mostly Russian studies in children comparing Diaskintest with the tuberculin skin test. It singles out a Brazilian Markov model study in people living with HIV as the only one meeting most quality criteria.

blocks.title: Page 967
blocks.content:
We evaluated study quality using the Drummond’s checklist for health economic evaluations (supplementary 
material, Table A7). On average, we identified that most studies did not present any sensitivity analysis, and 
that the information on relevant parameters such as time horizon, type of model used, year of the evaluation, 
and discounting rate were unclear, or not stated. Overall, study quality was concerning. 
 
Description of the articles in the secondary review (PPD-TST and IGRA)  
 
Of the 29 papers included in the review, 8 were based in the United Kingdom (UK), 6 in the United States

summary.text: Notes that most studies of the new skin tests lacked sensitivity analyses and clear model details, so their quality was concerning. It then describes the 29 studies on the tuberculin skin test and IGRA, mostly from high-income countries, which used various models and were generally of high quality.

blocks.title: Page 968
blocks.content:
compared strategies to DiaskinTest only. The dominance of DiaskinTest was very sensitive to unit costs of 
DiaskinTest which is highly uncertain due to using market value and hence varies widely by health system and 
country.  The rest of the articles found that the cost of the DiaskinTest kit ranged from $1.29 to $3.49 and that 
it was not very sensitive to unit costs after employing univariate sensitivity analyses (if measured). All these 
studies, apart from Steffen et al, found that DiaskinTest was cost-effective using a wide-range of methods, 
ranging from a cost-effectiveness ratio of 2.

summary.text: Summarizes findings that Diaskintest kits cost about $1.29–3.49 and that almost all studies judged it cost-effective compared with the tuberculin skin test, with results sensitive to unit costs. Table 1 gives unit costs of Diaskintest and C-TST from the primary review in 2021 US dollars.

blocks.title: Page 969
blocks.content:
Most studies evaluated the costs and cost-effectiveness of PPD-TST and IGRA with wide-ranging study 
populations including PLHIV, immunocompromised people other than PLHIV, immigrants/migrants, healthcare 
workers  and different methods were used, especially time horizons. 22 studies were set in low TB burden 
countries (UK, USA, Canada, Norway, Oman, Spain), 4 in lower moderate (Brazil, Japan, Singapore), 1 in upper-
moderate (Hong Kong) and two in a high burden country (South Africa). Four studies were based in low-and-
middle income countries, whereas 25 in high-income countries.  Most stud

summary.text: Summarizes the secondary review, noting that most studies were in low-burden, high-income countries and that testing was more likely to be cost-effective in high-risk groups or high-burden settings, without consensus on which test to use. It reports that studies in people living with HIV generally found IGRA more cost-effective, with one finding Diaskintest most cost-effective, and describes reasons for variation in unit costs.

Interpretation 
 
Considering the same factors (ingredients) for economic costing, costs of novel skin tests (DiaskinTest=$5.07, C-
TST=$9.9912) were substantially lower than those of IGRA (average cost was $89.33; ranging from $22.1712 to 
$247.1227) and the TST (average cost=$37.84, ranging from $4.4028 to $181.6324). However, in isolation, 
observed low costs of DiaskinTest and C-TST compared to TST and IGRA are not sufficient evidence for likely 
economic impact, particularly given the limited number of studies. More high-quality studies are needed (only 
one high-quality study found) cons

summary.text: Interprets the findings, noting that novel skin tests cost far less than IGRA or the tuberculin skin test but that low costs alone, from few and generally poor-quality studies in Russia and Brazil, do not show likely economic impact. It states that a modelling study was undertaken with results in Part B.

Extended Summary 
 
Background: Our systematic review on the economic impact of novel Mycobacterium tuberculosis specific skin 
tests for tuberculosis infection (TBST) conducted for this WHO meeting (Section A, Economic impact report) 
shows that studies are few and limited by study quality. However, our report does provide the most updated 
evidence on the cost-effectiveness of the use of TBST compared to currently used tests for tuberculosis 
infection. We aim to use this evidence to parameterise an economic modelling study to assess whether TBST 
are affordable and feasible to implement und

summary.text: The extended summary explains that a Markov model was built to compare the cost-effectiveness of new antigen-based skin tests with the PPD tuberculin skin test and IGRA in Brazil, South Africa and the UK, focusing on DiaskinTest because only its maker supplied costs. Costs are from a health system perspective, and sensitivity analyses explore test prices and uncertainty in clinical and utility parameters.

blocks.title: Page 1051
blocks.content:
Results: In Brazil, strategy 1 is cost saving compared to strategy 2 and 3. Compared to PPD-TST, DiaskinTest is 
cost-saving at $5.6 with an incremental gain of 0.024 QALYs per patient. Compared to IGRA, DiaskinTest is cost 
saving at $8.4 with an incremental gain of 0.01 QALYs. In South Africa, DST is more cost saving than IGRA and 
PPD-TST. Compared to PPD-TST, DiaskinTest is cost-saving at $4.39 with an incremental gain of 0.0152 QALYs. 
Compared to IGRA, DiaskinTest is cost saving at $64.41 with an incremental gain of 0.0065 QALYs. In the UK, 
strategy 1 is cost saving compared to strategy

summary.text: Reports that DiaskinTest was cost saving with small QALY gains against both comparators in Brazil and South Africa, and against the skin test but not IGRA in the UK, where it remained cost-effective, and sets out how far test prices could rise and stay cost saving. The interpretation stresses that results depend on country-specific costing and limited evidence and that other new skin tests could not be modelled for lack of cost data.

Model scheme and characteristics 
 
We created a Markov model simulating a cohort of individuals transitioning among different states, the cohort 
being comprised at baseline of individuals without active TB. Following the cascade of care, these individuals 
are tested for TB infection (TBI), if positive, they may initiate and eventually complete or interrupt treatment. 
Consequently, the model’s states are: (1) no tuberculosis infection, tested; (2) tuberculosis infection, tested; (3) 
no tuberculosis infection,

summary.text: Describes the Markov model, which follows a cohort without active TB through testing for infection, treatment, completion or interruption, active TB, recovery or death, across eleven states. It is parametrized for the UK, Brazil and South Africa, and the modelling objectives are restated.

blocks.content: Model diagram (Figure 1) of the TB infection care cascade. From a starting node 'Tested for TB infection', arrows branch to 'No TBI tested' (leading to 'No TBI treated', 'No TBI untreated' and 'No TBI Treatment interrupted') and 'TBI tested' (leading to 'TBI treated', 'TBI untreated' and 'TBI Treatment interrupted'). 'TBI treated' and 'TBI Treatment interrupted' both point to 'TBI untreated', which leads by a dashed arrow to 'Active TB'; each end state ends in a green triangle terminal node.

untreated; (8) tuberculosis infection, treatment started but interrupted; (9) active TB; (10) no TB; (11) death. We start with 
a cohort of individuals without TB.

3.2.4 Summary of Work Package B findings from User Interviews 
End user values and preferences 
Healthcare providers and consumers were found to value TBI test accuracy, convenience, a positive 
patient experience, low cost and resource requirements, and these factors affected their 
preferences for TBI tests. The novel antigen-based skin tests (TBSTs) were discussed as having 
comparable accuracy to the IGRA, however with better affordability and lower resource 
requirements. In comparison to the TSTs, the TBSTs were viewed to have better accuracy and 
comparable affordability, resource

summary.text: Summarizes the user interview findings: providers and consumers valued accuracy, convenience, a good patient experience, low cost and low resource needs. The new antigen-based skin tests were seen as matching IGRA accuracy at lower cost and resource needs, and as more accurate than the TST at similar cost. Interviewees cautioned that in low-income settings the TBST alone would not fix wider access barriers such as stock, staff training and equipment.

Conclusion 
In conclusion, TBST were deemed to be more acceptable and equally feasible to the TST, with 
greater benefits for health equity driven by higher sensitivity and specificity. TBST may be more 
preferable for use in more resource-limited settings compared to the TST. IGRA appears the 
preferred test option in high-income countries with the infrastructure to support their use; it is 
unlikely that widespread use of the IGRA would change in these settings. End-users were found to 
value attributes such as test accuracy, convenience, a positive patient experience, cost, and resour

summary.text: Concludes that antigen-based skin tests were judged more acceptable than and as feasible as the TST, with equity benefits, and possibly preferable in resource-limited settings, while IGRA remains favoured in high-income countries; these findings shaped the discrete choice experiment.

Introduction  
Tuberculosis (TB) is an airborne transmissible infectious disease caused by Mycobacterium 
tuberculosis. TB is a major cause of health loss (i.e., healthy life years lost to death, illness, or disability), 
affecting approximately one quarter of the global population and ranking as one of the top ten causes 
of death1. Approximately one quarter to one-third of the global population is estimated to have latent 
TB infection (TBI) 2, 3. TBI may progress to active disease, especially in those with pre-disposing factors 
such as HIV infection, diabetes, and immunosuppressive co

3.2.4 Summary of Work Package B findings from User Interviews 
End user values and preferences 
Healthcare providers and consumers were found to value TBI test accuracy, convenience, a positive 
patient experience, low cost and resource requirements, and these factors affected their 
preferences for TBI tests. The novel antigen-based skin tests (TBSTs) were discussed as having 
comparable accuracy to the IGRA, however with better affordability and lower resource 
requirements. In comparison to the TSTs, the TBSTs were viewed to have better accuracy and 
comparable affordability, resource

summary.text: Summarises interview findings that providers and consumers value accuracy, convenience, good patient experience, low cost and low resource needs. Novel skin tests were seen as similar in accuracy to IGRA but cheaper and less resource-intensive, and more accurate than the tuberculin skin test, though still needing a return visit. It adds that wider access barriers in low-income settings will not be solved by introducing the new tests alone.

blocks.title: Page 1161
blocks.content:

Conclusion 
In conclusion, TBST were deemed to be more acceptable and equally feasible to the TST, with 
greater benefits for health equity driven by higher sensitivity and specificity. TBST may be more 
preferable for use in more resource-limited settings compared to the TST. IGRA appears the 
preferred test option in high-income countries with the infrastructure to support their use; it is 
unlikely that widespread use of the IGRA would change in these settings. End-users were found to 
value attributes such as test accuracy, convenience, a positive patient experience, cost, and resour

summary.text: Concludes that novel skin tests were judged more acceptable than and as feasible as the tuberculin skin test, with greater equity benefits, while IGRA remains preferred in well-resourced high-income settings.
